about.name: Qiyu Li
paragraphs: I build AI-native tools and creative software around thinking, creating, and working with AI — mostly around human–AI interaction, visual systems, and turning messy ideas into things that actually work.
Outside the editor you'll usually find me around photography, films, table tennis, and whatever I'm curious about next.

principles: Human judgment stays in the loop.
Build the tools I wish already existed.

lines: Building tools for thinking, creating, and working with AI.
Turning messy ideas into systems that actually run.
Always building something I wish already existed.

_motionNote: Per-component switches so layout stays the author's decision. Each module has its OWN effect — 01 lights indicator keys, rhythm flickers at its meter ceilings, languages sweeps, the two list panels share a row highlight because they are a matched pair, contributions runs a diagonal wave, work marches a selection marquee. `ambient: false` keeps entrances but stops the never-ending ones; `enabled: false` makes the whole page static. Every animated file also carries a prefers-reduced-motion guard, and no effect may start from opacity 0 — see lib/motion.mjs.
_contactNote: A README cannot run script — GitHub strips it — so copy-to-clipboard on click is not possible on this page. EMAIL uses mailto:, which hands the click to whatever the reader's machine uses for mail without printing the address as text. WECHAT links to a QR stripped of the avatar, display name and city that came with it. WEBSITE stays off until yunmin311.github.io actually serves something; it currently 404s.
fortunes: The tool you keep meaning to build is the one you need most.
A system nobody can explain is a system nobody can fix.
Autocomplete is not agreement.
Ship the ugly version. The pretty one never arrives on its own.
Every abstraction is a promise you will have to keep later.
If it only works when you are watching, it does not work.
Good defaults beat good documentation.
The messy draft already knows what the clean one is trying to say.
A model can hold the context. It cannot hold the responsibility.
Name it badly and you will build it badly.
Delete the feature you keep apologising for.
The best interface is the one you stop noticing.
Constraints are the part of the brief that survives contact with reality.
You cannot automate a decision you have never made by hand.
Any pipeline long enough contains one step nobody understands.
Taste is just the errors you have already made, remembered.
If the demo needs narration, the design is not finished.
Prototypes are arguments. Ship the one that wins.
Most 'AI problems' are unclear-input problems wearing a costume.
Two hours of naming things saves two weeks of explaining them.
_projectsNote: THE SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for both SELECTED WORK and LANGUAGE SIGNAL. There is no second repository list anywhere: the cards and the language chart are both derived from this array by scripts/lib/projects.mjs. LANGUAGE SIGNAL counts exactly the projects currently SHOWN as cards, so the chart is always a caption on the grid above it — never on projects the reader cannot see. THE RULE, IN THREE STATES: tier 'core' = strongly preferred, leads a comparison by coreLeadDays, then competes on merit like everything else and RETAINS THE ABILITY TO RETIRE; tier 'candidate' = no preference beyond the stability guard; `pinned` (top level) = genuinely permanent, never retires — the ONLY way to say 'always on the page', and a deliberate hand-edit rather than a side effect of being important. ORDERING: recency (days since my last commit, weight 0.6, linear over 180 days) plus volume (log10 of lines I wrote, weight 0.4). Deliberately NOT stars, forks or raw commit counts. languages: 'count' = contributes to LANGUAGE SIGNAL, 'exclude' = real code but distorting (generated or vendored), 'n/a' = nothing comparable to count; a project unsuitable for language stats must be declared HERE, never dropped into a second list. DYNAMIC: the cards' member set and order, and the chart's numbers AND its scope. CURATED, changing only when this file changes: every word on a card.

projects.name: Context Distiller
projects.why: Choosing what an AI gets to see is the step nobody built a tool for. A workspace for picking, grouping and compiling that context into one plain-text message — locally, and never sent anywhere.

projects.name: Governance Framework
projects.why: Run several AI agents and they forget, contradict each other, and disagree about which file is real. Pinning the facts into files fixes what a smarter model cannot.

projects.name: Yunmin Workbench
projects.why: A clean-room desktop workbench for running Claude Code and Codex side by side — rebuilt from a frozen baseline rather than patched forward, because a tool you depend on has to be explainable.

projects.name: DSH Universal Palette
projects.why: Three products with three different colour systems, and a designer retyping hex codes between them. One plugin turns whatever you are looking at into the palette you actually use.

projects.name: Window Annotator
projects.why: Drawing on the thing you are looking at should not depend on the app supporting it. Hand-drawn marks pin to any Windows window and follow it as it moves, resizes and scrolls.

projects.name: Zheng Tally for Obsidian
projects.why: Counting things in a note should not mean leaving the note. Tally marks you can strike through inline, with the running total kept where the writing happens.

projects.name: Work Capsule
projects.why: Keeping work in sync across machines should not risk it. One click pulls, optionally commits and pushes every folder you chose — fast-forward only, never rewriting history.

projects.name: Pixel Panels
projects.why: The components this page is built from, lifted out and documented. One 2px grid, one embedded bitmap face, and the four rules that keep fourteen separate parts reading as a single instrument.

projects.name: DenseGPT
projects.why: A long answer you cannot scan is a long answer nobody reads. One stylesheet tightens the reading layout and the content width; a companion spec asks the model for answers shaped to fit it.

_policyNote: EVERY NUMBER HERE IS INITIAL POLICY, NOT AN EMPIRICAL RESULT. They were chosen to be reasonable, deterministic and easy to change — nothing was fitted to anything and none of them should be treated as settled. THE FOUR KNOBS, and what to turn: `hysteresisDays` is how many days fresher a challenger must be before it takes a card from what is already there — raise it if cards flicker in and out, lower it if a card you expect to see cannot get in. `coreLeadDays` is the head start `tier: 'core'` gets — raise it if a core project drops off, lower it if one is overstaying. `stalenessToleranceDays` is when the page admits the rule has drifted and fails the build — it affects reporting only, never what is displayed. `pinned` is not a number: it is the list of keys that never retire.
_languageScopeNote: HOW the language chart counts — not WHICH repositories. Scope is derived from `projects` above by lib/projects.mjs, so there is no repository list to keep in sync here. `identities` is matched case-insensitively against each commit's author email AND name; add an entry when a new machine commits under a different address, or those commits disappear from the chart with no error at all — the quietest way this panel can be wrong. `exclude` drops generated and vendored languages from the line count: the chart claims 'lines I wrote', and markup or lockfile churn is not writing. `method` is 'authored-lines' (clone each repo, count my insertions) and degrades to 'bytes' automatically if cloning fails; the panel prints which one is in force, because the two measure different things.
